question.text: Ms. Kavita Raghavan, the sponsor of a proposed Category II AIF, is debating whether to adopt a trust, LLP, or company structure. From a manager's liability and investor flexibility perspective, why do majority of Indian AIFs adopt a trust structure?

answer.text: Trust structure eliminates the need for SEBI registration
Trust permits ring-fencing of manager's liability since manager is only a counterparty service provider, unlike being on the board of a company or a designated partner of an LLP
A trust has a separate legal personality distinct from the trustee
Trusts are exempt from paying GST on management fees

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 13.3, a trust structure permits ring fencing of the manager's liability (including fiduciary and breach of fund documents perspective) from that of the AIF because the manager is only a counterparty service provider to the AIF, unlike being on the board of directors of a company AIF or a designated partner of an LLP. This is why majority AIFs in India are constituted as trusts. The Trap: Trust does NOT have a separate legal personality (it's a relationship). SEBI registration is required regardless of structure. GST applies uniformly. The real driver is liability ring-fencing. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A tests AIF structures conceptually; XIX-C drills into the manager-side liability implications of each form. Compare with XXI-B (PMS), where structure debate doesn't arise — PMS is always a contractual relationship. Manager's Pro-Tip: Even in a trust, consider an LLP as the manager entity (not the fund) — gives the sponsor personal liability ring-fencing against potential 'for-cause' litigation by LPs.
